items.heading: Video 5.1 | Data Privacy
items.paragraph: This lesson introduces the module and turns the focus from how to use GenAI toward the risks of misusing it. Participants will gain an understanding of what can go wrong through real-world cases, such as leaked trade secrets and fabricated legal citations. The module's learning goals and key risks—data privacy, hallucinations, and bias—are previewed.

items.title: Audio description transcript - Course Overview
items.description:
[Visual description]: Text appears: The InnovateUS Logo.

[Visual description]: Title card: Responsible AI for Public Professionals: Understanding Risks and Building Resilience.

[Visual description]: Title card: Understanding Risks.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Ariana Escanlante, presenter, InnovateUS.


Welcome back. In our prior videos, we've focused on what to do. Now let's turn to the risks and what not to do.


[Visual description]: Image appears: a screenshot of the Forbes article titled: Samsung Bans ChatGPT Among Employees After Sensitive Code Leak. 

Like any tool, GenAI can be misused. You might have heard a story about an employee typing trade secrets into ChatGPT.

[Visual description]: Image appears: a screenshot of the CNBC article titled: Judge sanctions lawyers for brief written by A.I. with fake citations.

 Or the lawyer who let GenAI write his legal brief — resulting in fabricated case citations submitted to a court.

[Visual description]: Title card: Learning Goals.


By the end of this module, you will:

Have a deeper understanding of the risks associated with GenAI use

Have a set of ethical guidelines to ensure you work responsibly with GenAI

Know practical strategies for overcoming those risks


[Visual description]: Title card: What we’ll cover.

We focus on risks specific to your own use of these tools at work, including data privacy, hallucinations, and bias and how to assess and avoid each. Later on we'll address broader societal issues like copyright.


Of course, our advice is not a substitute for your agency's specific policies. Let's dive in.

items.heading: Video 5.1 | Data Privacy
items.paragraph: The module addresses the responsible use of GenAI by discussing potential risks and mitigation strategies. Data privacy, hallucinations, and bias are introduced as key challenges. Participants learn to assess and avoid these risks through practical guidance and organizational policies.

items.title: Audio description transcript - Data Privacy
items.description:
[Visual description]: Text appears: The InnovateUS Logo

[Visual description]: Title card: Responsible AI for Public Professionals: Understanding Risks and Building Resilience.

[Visual description]: Title card: Data Privacy.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Ariana Escanlante, presenter, InnovateUS

As with any software or website, the privacy of what you input into GenAI tools is governed by the software's terms of use, which vary by platform and your organization’s contract. 

[Visual description]: Title card: Privacy.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Read the ‘Terms of Use’ and check with legal counsel.

It's always advisable to read those terms and check with legal counsel when in doubt.

As a general rule, free versions of popular GenAI tools may use what you input to train and improve their technology. Assume you have limited privacy on these platforms.

[Visual description]: Image appears: An AI siphoning data from a user's computer while saying “Feed me your data” and “I’m free, you pay me with your data!”, generated by Canva.

[Visual description]: Title card: Enterprise Licences.

Enterprise-wide licenses offered by major services often provide greater privacy protection, including limiting the reuse of your data. You should always check with your IT department regarding what's approved in your organization before using any AI tool, and especially before inputting any personally-identifiable information about residents, colleagues, or yourself.

[Visual description]: Title card: Privacy.

Unless using an approved tool and  your agency policy permits otherwise (many do)

Do not share internal memos, documents not cleared for publication, sensitive data

Do not include personally identifiable information about residents, colleagues, or yourself

Do not share passwords, private keys, or proprietary details

Don't share anything you wouldn't share publicly

One more consideration: even when using an approved AI assistant, in many jurisdictions, your prompts and GenAI outputs may be subject to public records laws, freedom of information law requests, or records retention requirements — just like email or other official communications. Some agencies also require that AI-assisted work products be logged or disclosed.

These tools are excellent for transcribing and summarizing audio recordings. But be mindful that meeting transcriptions may also be subject to retention and disclosure laws.

And, of course, make sure you have consent before recording or transcribing any meeting, especially involving sensitive or confidential topics.

lessons.title: Self Assessment 1.1

items.title: What steps should you take to ensure responsible use of generative AI tools from a privacy perspective? (Select all that apply)

answers.title: A. Read and understand the terms and conditions of the tool
B. Consult with legal counsel if you have doubts or questions
C. Share sensitive information to test the tool's privacy measures
D. Assume the tool has strong privacy protections without checking

items.feedbackIncorrect: The correct answers are A and B. To ensure responsible use of generative AI tools from a privacy perspective, you should read and understand the terms and conditions of the tool and consult with legal counsel if you have doubts or questions.

items.title: How do free generative AI tools differ from paid versions in terms of data usage?

answers.title: Free and paid versions use the input data in exactly the same way
answers.feedback: Free and paid versions often have different data usage policies, with paid versions typically offering more privacy.

answers.title: Free versions use the data to train the AI, while all paid versions do not use the data at all
answers.feedback: While paid versions may offer more privacy, they may still use some data for AI improvement.

answers.title: Enterprise or organizational licenses often (but not always) offer greater privacy protection for input data
Enterprise versions sell the input data to third-party advertisers, while free versions do not
answers.feedback: Enterprise versions generally offer more privacy protections, not increased data selling to third parties.

items.title: What type of data should you avoid inputting into generative AI tools?

answers.title: Publicly available information from official sources
Sensitive data, such as personally identifiable information
General knowledge and facts that are not specific to individuals
Information about upcoming public events and announcements

items.heading: Video 5.2 | Hallucinations
items.paragraph: Hallucinations, or inaccurate outputs, are explored in depth. Strategies to identify and mitigate hallucinations are provided, including using multiple models, temperature settings, and retrieval-augmented generation. The importance of fact-checking and iterative improvement is emphasized.

items.title: Audio description transcript - Hallucinations and Accuracy
items.description:
[Visual description]: Text appears: The InnovateUS Logo.

[Visual description]: Title card: Responsible AI for Public Professionals: Understanding Risks and Building Resilience.

[Visual description]: Title card: Hallucinations and Accuracy.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Ariana Escanlante, presenter, InnovateUS.

Generative AI can sound confident even when it is wrong. 

[Visual description]: Image appears: a screenshot of The Markup article titled: NYC’s AI Chatbot Tells Businesses to Break the Law.

One city’s business chatbot, for example, was reported to give incorrect legal guidance—such as suggesting employers could withhold workers’ tips—and a subsequent audit found instances of inaccurate and inconsistent responses.

Why do hallucinations happen? 

[Visual description]: Title card: What is a hallucination?

Generative AI creates responses based on patterns in language, which means it can produce text that is fluent, confident, and false. This is often called a “hallucination.”

These systems have improved, but the problem has not disappeared. Error rates vary by platform, task, and prompt—and they change as models are updated. When accuracy matters, treat AI output as a starting point and verify it against authoritative sources.

[Visual description]: Title card: Hallucinations.

What can you do about hallucinations?

First, try more than one tool. If you run the same prompt in different systems, you can compare the answers—like getting a second opinion.

Second, use tools that show their sources. Some systems combine AI with web search and give you citations, which makes it easier to check their claims.

Third, when possible, use tools that are grounded in specific data—like a set of official documents or policies. That can reduce errors, though it doesn’t eliminate them.

Fourth, be clear in how you ask. More specific prompts usually lead to better results.

[Visual description]: Image appears: a screenshot of the IEEE Spectrum article titled: AI Models Fail Miserably at This One Easy Task: Telling Time.

And finally, check the output. AI models may write a flawless memo but they  cannot reliably tell time

Think of it like reviewing work from a junior colleague—you still need to verify before you rely on it.

When you’re checking AI output, there are a few simple things to look for.

If it cites a study or a statistic, take a moment to find the original source.

Fabricated or misattributed citations do happen. If it names an author, make sure that person actually exists—and that they really wrote what’s being attributed to them.

For important claims, cross-check against a reliable source you trust.

And if the tool gives you a link, click it. AI-generated URLs can look convincing but sometimes lead nowhere.

Finally, you can also ask the tool directly: Are you confident this is accurate? What’s your source? It won’t always fix the problem, but it can surface useful clues.

One practical point: AI outputs can change from one run to the next. For official work, keep a record of what the tool produced and what you changed.

Next up: let's talk about bias.

lessons.title: Self Assessment 1.2

items.title: What is the term used to describe the phenomenon of generative AI tools producing false or inaccurate information?

answers.title: Deception
answers.feedback: Deception implies intentional misleading, which is not the case with generative AI hallucinations.

answers.title: Hallucination
Bias
answers.feedback: While bias can contribute to inaccurate outputs, the specific phenomenon described here is known as hallucination.

answers.title: Glitch
answers.feedback: A glitch suggests a temporary malfunction, whereas hallucination is a byproduct of the AI's language modeling approach.

items.title: What is the primary reason generative AI tools can sometimes produce false or inaccurate information?

answers.title: They intentionally deceive users by generating false information
answers.feedback: Generative AI tools do not intentionally deceive users, but can produce inaccurate information due to their probabilistic nature.

answers.title: They generate responses based on patterns in language, which can produce text that sounds convincing but is actually false
They are programmed to occasionally generate false information to test user attentiveness
answers.feedback: False information is not intentionally generated to test users, but is a byproduct of the AI's language modeling approach.

answers.title: They have a built-in bias towards generating false information
answers.feedback: The generation of false information is not due to a built-in bias, but rather a result of the probabilistic language modeling technique.

items.title: Why is using more than one AI model helpful for spotting hallucinations?

answers.title: Different models will always produce the same hallucinations
answers.feedback: Different models are likely to produce different hallucinations, not the same ones.

answers.title: Comparing outputs from multiple models can highlight inconsistencies and potential inaccuracies
Using multiple models guarantees the complete elimination of hallucinations
answers.feedback: While using multiple models can help identify hallucinations, it does not guarantee their complete elimination.

answers.title: Multiple models are required to generate any output at all
answers.feedback: Multiple models are not required to generate output, but rather serve as a means of comparison to identify potential issues.

items.title: What is the most important step when using generative AI tools?

answers.title: Blindly trusting the AI-generated output without review
answers.feedback: Blindly trusting AI output without review can lead to the use of inaccurate or inappropriate information.

answers.title: Checking and proofreading the results generated by the AI
Assuming the AI output is always inferior to human-generated content
answers.feedback: While human oversight is important, assuming AI output is always inferior can lead to underutilization of these tools.

answers.title: Avoiding the use of generative AI tools in all circumstances
answers.feedback: Generative AI tools can be helpful when used responsibly, so avoiding them altogether may not be the best approach.

items.heading: Video 5.3 | Bias
items.paragraph: Bias in GenAI is discussed, stemming from biased training data. Examples illustrate how GenAI can replicate societal biases. Techniques to correct for bias, such as targeted prompting and manual correction, are introduced, along with the potential for GenAI to help identify bias.

items.title: Audio description transcript - Bias
items.description:
[Visual description]: Text appears: The InnovateUS Logo

[Visual description]: Title card: Responsible AI for Public Professionals: Using GenAI in Government.

[Visual description]: Title card: Bias.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Ariana Escanlante, presenter, InnovateUS.

Welcome back. We’ve looked at hallucinations—now let’s turn to bias.

[Visual description]: Image appears: A scale leveraging Bias against Facts within a person's head, generated by ChatGPT5.5.

Bias in AI means outputs are not neutral—they can advantage some groups and disadvantage others. In government, that can lead to unequal treatment, flawed decisions, and reduced trust.

The root of this bias lies in the training data. GenAI is trained on vast amounts of text from the internet — the good and the bad.

[Visual description]: Data with “Bias In” written on it enters a visual representation of a Gen AI, and it then outputs data with “Bias Out” written on it.

Generative AI does not create bias from scratch; it learns patterns in the data and can reproduce or amplify them.

For example, when asked to generate or evaluate resumes, a model may produce different responses for otherwise identical candidates based only on names, reflecting patterns of bias found in human decision-making.

[Visual description]: Two CVs are reviewed by a Gen AI, one of the CVs is passed, and the other is labeled Fail.

Even with balanced training data, bias can also arise from how the model generalizes patterns. If training data overrepresents certain pathways to success—such as graduates of a small set of prestigious universities—the model may reflect those patterns even when they are not relevant.

AI researchers are working to reduce bias through techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, where models are trained to avoid harmful or stereotypical outputs. But because these systems learn from real-world data, bias cannot be fully eliminated.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Disclaimer: The commercial tools mentioned in this course are for illustrative purposes and do not imply endorsement by InnovateUS.

You can sometimes correct for bias directly. If you ask for an image of a lawyer and get only one gender or race, ask for alternatives. 

[Visual description]: The AI first generates an image of a white male lawyer. When asked to provide alternatives with different genders and races, it creates four images of lawyers with various racial backgrounds, of which 3 are female.

You can also ask GenAI to review text or images for potential bias, and some tools are designed specifically for that purpose. Still, these are not perfect detectors and require human judgment.

[Visual description]: When asked to generate an image of a doctor without bias on race or gender, the AI provides two images containing a female doctor.

Bias also appears in translation. Quality is generally strong for widely spoken languages, but it can be weaker for less-resourced languages, including many indigenous languages. This can lead to inaccurate or culturally inappropriate results. When translating for these communities, always have a fluent speaker review the output.

Bias is not always easy to detect. Although Generative AI systems can provide explanations, these do not reliably reflect how the model produced its output, making problematic patterns difficult to identify.

[Visual description]: When asked to explain the reasoning behind an answer, the AI does not mention bias in its analysis of its own response.

This is one reason policymakers have placed limits on high-risk uses of AI, especially in areas like employment, education, and access to services.

[Visual description]: Image appears: a screenshot of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. Chapter: High-Risk AI Systems.

The takeaway is straightforward: be thoughtful about the tasks you assign to GenAI, and stay in control of decisions that affect people.

[Visual description]: Image appears: a screenshot of the White House paper titled: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust.

At the same time, GenAI can also help identify bias—if used carefully. You can ask it to flag potentially biased language or outputs for you to correct, but the final judgment must remain with you.

In our final video in this section, we'll discuss strategies for mitigating all these risks.

lessons.title: Self Assessment 1.3

items.title: What does it mean when we say that generative AI "reflects the bias that created it"?

answers.title: The AI tools actively create new biases that did not exist before
answers.feedback: Generative AI tools do not create entirely new biases, but rather reflect and perpetuate existing ones.

answers.title: The AI learns patterns from its training data and can reproduce or even amplify biases present in that data
The AI tools eliminate all biases and produce perfectly neutral outputs
answers.feedback: While AI tools can be helpful, they are not capable of eliminating all biases and producing perfectly neutral outputs.

answers.title: The AI tools only reflect the biases of their current users, not their training data
answers.feedback: The biases in AI outputs are primarily a reflection of the training data, not just the biases of current users.

items.title: What makes it challenging to identify bias in generative AI outputs?

answers.title: The transparent and easily understandable nature of AI decision-making processes
answers.feedback: AI decision-making processes are often complex and opaque, not transparent and easily understandable.

answers.title: The lack of bias in the data used to train AI models
answers.feedback: Bias in AI outputs often stems from biases present in the training data, not a lack of bias in the data.

answers.title: The complexity and unclear nature of AI decision-making processes
The absence of any bias in AI-generated outputs
answers.feedback: Bias can exist in AI-generated outputs, and the challenge lies in identifying and addressing it.

items.title: What is an example of a task that you should be cautious about asking generative AI to perform?

answers.title: Generating a summary of a publicly available research article
answers.feedback: Summarizing a publicly available research article is generally a low-risk task for AI, as long as the output is reviewed for accuracy.

answers.title: Producing a transcript of a public meeting recording
answers.feedback: Transcribing a public meeting recording is typically a suitable task for AI, provided no sensitive information is shared.

answers.title: Making a decision or recommendation that significantly impacts people's lives
Creating a first draft of a non-sensitive document for internal review
answers.feedback: Generating a first draft of a non-sensitive document for internal review is an appropriate use of AI, as long as the output is reviewed and edited by humans.

items.heading: Video 5.4 | Mitigating Risks
items.paragraph: Five crucial behaviors for responsible GenAI use are presented: continuous learning, evaluation, maintaining human control, transparency, and prioritizing low-risk applications. The video emphasizes the importance of risk reduction while comparing to the risk of existing processes.

items.title: Audio description transcript - Mitigating Risks Responsibly
items.description:
[Visual description]: Text appears: The InnovateUS Logo.

[Visual description]: Title card: Responsible AI for Public Professionals: Understanding Risks and Building Resilience.

[Visual description]: Title card: Mitigating Risks Responsibly.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Ariana Escanlante, presenter, InnovateUS.


Welcome back! Responsible use of GenAI, requires adherence to five crucial behaviors:

Staying current on best practices by learning from others

Critically assessing every output

Maintaining human control…AI on Tap, not on Top

Being transparent and always disclosing your use of GenAI

Prioritizing lower-risk applications

You've already started learning by taking this course!. To keep improving, focus on three things: practice, policy, and peer learning.

Use these tools regularly on real work so you build intuition for what works.

Make sure you understand your organization’s rules on data security and approved tools before using them.

And learn from others—share effective prompts and workflows with colleagues, and adopt what works.

When evaluating outputs, work on tasks within your area of expertise so you can assess quality and accuracy. Ask yourself: could I defend this to a colleague? Use more than one tool to compare results, and never treat GenAI as a substitute for human judgment. For example, don’t publish public-facing content or even send around a draft of a memo without carefully reviewing it first.

Be transparent. Clearly label when content has been created or assisted by AI, whether for internal or public use. Document the tools, prompts, and methods you used so others can understand and replicate your work.

In some cases, accessibility accommodations may affect disclosure requirements, for example, employees using AI-powered assistive tools. Consult your agency's legal counsel or disability services office if you have questions about whether an exemption applies to your situation.

Prioritize low-risk uses. There is less risk in using GenAI to draft internal materials that will be reviewed than in generating content residents rely on for critical decisions. Always build in human oversight.

This is sometimes described as “AI on tap, not on top.” GenAI can support your work, but the responsibility and accountability remain with you—especially for high-stakes outcomes that affect people’s lives.

Transparency also builds trust. Residents increasingly expect to know when AI is used in government services or communications. Clear disclosure helps maintain credibility and allows errors to be identified and corrected.

Remember: there is no such thing as zero risk. The goal is to reduce risk. When evaluating GenAI, compare it to current practice—does it improve accuracy, consistency, or fairness? Human processes are not error-free either, so the question is whether these tools help us do better.

Finally, if your organization hasn't yet approved any AI tools, that's not uncommon. Consider raising the conversation with your supervisor. You can make the case by sharing what you've learned in this course about potential benefits and safeguards needed. Many organizations have started with a limited pilot on a single approved platform before expanding.


In the past few videos, we covered:

Privacy, hallucination, and bias

Practical ways to mitigate these risks

Next, we’ll look at broader societal challenges.

lessons.title: Self Assessment 1.4

items.title: Why is it recommended to use generative AI for tasks within your area of expertise?

answers.title: To maximize the entertainment value and popularity of the AI's outputs
answers.feedback: The primary reason for focusing on tasks within your expertise is to ensure quality and accuracy, not to maximize entertainment value.

answers.title: To eliminate the need for any human review or oversight of the AI's outputs
answers.feedback: Using AI for tasks within your expertise still requires human review and oversight to ensure the best results.

answers.title: To challenge yourself to work on projects outside of your comfort zone
answers.feedback: While challenging yourself can be valuable, the main purpose of this recommendation is to leverage your expertise for effective AI use.

answers.title: To ensure you have the skills and knowledge to assess the quality and accuracy of the AI's outputs

items.title: Why is it important to disclose the use of AI, even when it is used sparingly?

answers.title: To mislead people about the extent of AI involvement in a project
answers.feedback: Disclosing AI use is about transparency, not misleading people about the extent of AI involvement.

answers.title: To exaggerate the capabilities and reliability of AI tools
answers.feedback: The purpose of disclosure is to provide accurate information about AI use, not to exaggerate its capabilities.

answers.title: To foster trust and facilitate error identification
To discourage people from engaging with AI-generated content
answers.feedback: Disclosing AI use aims to promote informed engagement, not discourage people from interacting with AI-generated content.
